Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[reference notes]
North Quay is a fictional regional depot beside the old ferry terminal. It handles boxed maintenance parts, packaged dry goods, and replacement fixtures for six smaller depots along the coast. The receiving office is in a converted ticket hall, where shift leads record arrivals before drivers move pallets into the covered bays. The depot's weekly operations briefing usually includes a short section on received deliveries, because supervisors want to understand what the reporting query is intended to count before discussing it with the warehouse team.

The data table named deliveries is used in an example query shared by the reporting group. Its column names in that snippet are depot_id, units, and status. The reporting group has not supplied a schema, sample rows, database version, or definitions beyond those names. At the last planning meeting, analyst Mara Venn said, “The example is small on purpose; we need to discuss what the lines ask for, not pretend we know the whole system.” She asked the depot coordinator to keep the discussion focused on the query itself rather than on imagined dashboards or delivery records.

North Quay has several receiving routines, but the code below is the only query supplied for this review. In a normal week, one clerk checks carrier paperwork at the east desk while another weighs returned crates near bay four. Those routines are not represented in the snippet. The training handout is meant for supervisors who can read a basic SQL statement but may not recognize how filtering and grouping interact. A useful explanation should stay grounded in the visible names and operators and should distinguish what the query expresses from details the notes do not establish.

The supplied query is:
SELECT depot_id, SUM(units) AS received_units
FROM deliveries
WHERE status = 'received' AND units > 42
GROUP BY depot_id;

At a Thursday review, shift lead Tomas Rhee brought a marked-up printout to the briefing room. He said, “I can follow the depot grouping, but I want to be sure we explain the two conditions together, not as if either one were the whole filter.” He had seen staff confuse the word received in a report title with every delivery that had arrived during a shift. The team has no sample output to settle such questions, so the review should not claim a total, name a depot with the highest amount, or describe a particular row as included.

The briefing materials also mention that package sizes vary. Some carriers record units as individual items, while others use a standard carton quantity entered by the receiving clerk. The notes do not say whether units can be fractional, null, duplicated, or corrected after entry. Nor do they establish whether depot_id is always present or whether status can take values other than received. These open details are reasons to keep any proposed tests tied to the query's visible behavior and to identify assumptions rather than silently filling them in.

A separate discussion in the same meeting concerned how the example might be reviewed by a new supervisor. Mara suggested asking what rows pass the WHERE clause, what is combined by SUM, and what role GROUP BY depot_id plays in the selected result. Tomas wanted the review to note that received_units is an alias in the SELECT list, not a separate table column established by the notes. They agreed that any explanation should be readable aloud in about two minutes and should avoid claims about performance, indexes, or the report's business accuracy, since no supporting system information was provided.

1. The monthly briefing is assembled from handouts submitted by the six coastal depots. North Quay's copy is due to the coordinator on the first working day after month-end. If the review is completed before the Friday printing cutoff, the coordinator can include it in the supervisor packet; if it is not, it will be saved for the next packet. This timing affects only where the discussion note is filed, not what the SQL means or what test cases can be suggested.
2. The depot's training room has a whiteboard with three headings: “filter,” “aggregate,” and “group.” In the last session, a new supervisor asked whether a value of exactly 42 satisfies the visible units condition. The group did not resolve broader questions about how the source system stores units. A proposed test can use a boundary value to examine the written condition, but should not imply that the example describes a real delivery or a verified database result.
3. The reporting group has asked for a practical review that could be reused in a short onboarding session. They want the query's apparent intent explained in plain language, a concise review of the combination of conditions and grouping, and a few test ideas that could be checked if suitable sample data were later made available. The session is not an authorization to execute the query, change its text, or draw conclusions about actual depot activity.

In the final handout, the coordinator plans to place the explanation beside a map showing the ferry terminal, the covered bays, and the six coastal routes. The map is for orientation only and does not add evidence about the table or the query. A quote from clerk Nia Solberg is penciled into the margin: “If we say what we can see, people can ask better questions about what we still need to learn.” The review should keep that distinction in view, and the briefing remains conditional on the Friday printing cutoff described above. The query itself is the complete code supplied for the requested explanation, review, and test suggestions.
